opus-5.5.text:
Ha, well, I think it's partly a provocation, but I actually mean it. When people make a Mount Rushmore of scientists, they usually pick figures whose work is already canonized: Darwin, Watson and Crick, Barbara McClintock. That's looking backwards. What I care about is who's going to define the next era of biology, and I genuinely think some of those people are walking the halls at Arc right now.

Part of why we started Arc was a belief that the way we organize science limits what kinds of discoveries are possible. In the traditional academic model, you have brilliant people spending enormous fractions of their time writing grants, managing small labs in isolation, and optimizing for papers rather than for the hardest, most important problems. We wanted a place where people could take on long-horizon, high-risk projects and where biologists, computational people, and engineers actually work side by side every day, not just co-author a paper once in a while.

When you build that kind of environment, you see people do things that would have been very hard elsewhere. Take the work with Brian Hie and the team on Evo, training foundation models on DNA at genome scale so you can start to reason about and even design biological sequences across the central dogma. That's a fundamentally new way of doing biology. Or my co-founder Silvana Konermann, who's thinking about how to engineer cells and understand disease in ways that combine deep experimental craft with new tools. Then there are the people building virtual cell models and new experimental platforms that generate data at a scale we've never had.

So my answer is that a Mount Rushmore shouldn't just honor what's already been done. It should be a bet on who's changing how science gets done. I'd rather put my chips on the people I see taking those swings every day. And honestly, if I'm wrong, at least it'll make for a fun argument in ten years.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, well, I think the honest answer is that the Mount Rushmore framing is a bit of a joke, but there's something real underneath it. When Silvana and I started Arc, the whole premise was that the biggest bottleneck in biology isn't ideas, it's the structure around the people who have them. So we went out and tried to recruit folks who we genuinely thought were among the best in the world at what they do, and then gave them long-term, no-strings funding so they could actually swing for the fences.

So when I say my colleagues belong on that mountain, it's partly that I've gotten to watch them up close. Dave Burke, who did Evo with us, is thinking about genomes the way a language model thinks about text, and that's not a metaphor he borrowed, it's something he built. Hani Goodarzi and Chris Walsh and the rest of the core investigators are each attacking a problem that most labs would consider career-ending to even attempt. Being around that every day changes your sense of what's possible.

And frankly, I think the field undervalues the scientists who are doing the work right now. We canonize Darwin and Mendel and McClintock, and we should, but the people who are going to solve Alzheimer's or figure out how to read and write the genome at scale are alive and probably underfunded. So part of why I say it is to make a point: if you had to bet on who's going to matter in fifty years, I'd bet on the people down the hall from me. That's not loyalty, that's what I'd argue is a well-calibrated prior.

astra-6.text:
Because the people you work with closely shape how you think in a way that someone you admire from a distance rarely can. You see how they choose a problem, how they respond when an experiment fails, and how willing they are to question their own assumptions. That’s where you really learn what it means to be a scientist.

For me, putting my colleagues at Arc on that list is also about recognizing that science is a collective endeavor. We tend to tell stories about individual discoveries, but so much of the work comes from people challenging each other, sharing ideas, and making connections that none of them would have made alone. Those are the people who inspire me every day.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’m biased, of course, because I get to work with them. But what I admire is the combination of scientific ambition and a willingness to build something together. It’s one thing to have an exciting idea; it’s another to create the tools, the teams, and the environment that let people pursue ideas that might take years to pay off.

For me, that’s what makes a scientist worth celebrating: they change what other people can discover. And those are the kinds of colleagues I want to surround myself with.
